Common.title: Chain Lens — learn by reading transactions
Common.description: A learning tool for reading real blockchain transactions: what is public, what is encrypted, and what was never written. The read-only parts need no wallet and no private key.

samples.title: Start by reading these two
samples.lead: On 13 August 2026 a IIIF manifest for Saitan hokku-cho (1682), held by the National Diet Library of Japan, was registered in the dataspace portal Clio-X. The final screen (STEP 6, "Submit") lists three steps, but only steps 1 and 3 write to the chain. Step 2 is encryption and never touches it. Both transactions are still on the public chain.

create.title: 1. Create Tokens & Pricing
create.note: The screen says: "The Data NFT representing your asset, the Datatokens defining access to it, and the pricing schema are all created in a single transaction." It deployed three contracts and emitted fifteen records.

metadata.title: 3. Publish DDO
metadata.note: The screen says: "The encrypted DDO is stored on-chain as part of the Data NFT." Only two records, and just one of them carries content — encrypted.

what.title: How this differs from a general explorer
what.lead: For browsing transactions and balances, Etherscan is better. This tool only covers the three things it does not.

a.title: What if it had gone into storage?
a.body: The same bytes, priced as contract storage. The order-of-magnitude gap is the reason the design looks the way it does.

b.title: Open the data: URI in place
b.body: You are taught that an NFT points to an external JSON file. Not always. Here it is decoded for you.

c.title: Plain, encrypted, absent
c.body: What anyone can read, what nobody can, and what was never written. This is the part that matters in practice.

safety.title: On safety
safety.body: This tool only reads. There is no field for a private key. It never asks you to connect a wallet. It works on the Sepolia testnet only.

Inspect.title: Read a transaction
Inspect.description: Read one transaction recorded on an Ethereum testnet and sort out what stays in plain text, what is encrypted, and what was never written at all.

safe.title: This page only reads
safe.noKey: There is no field for a private key

result.summaryLead: Who sent it, where to, and what they paid — the information written on the envelope. It is always recorded, whatever the contents are. The contents appear further down under "Every event".

cf.title: What if it had gone into storage?
cf.lead: The largest piece of data here sits in an event log, not in contract storage. Here is what the same bytes would have cost in storage.
cf.conclusion: Writing {bytes} bytes to storage costs about {ratio}x what the log cost.
cf.source: Rates: Ethereum Yellow Paper / EIP-2929. SSTORE assumes a zero-to-nonzero write.

inv.title: Sorting what remains
inv.absentNote: The data itself is not on chain. Decrypting item 2 would reveal the title and file URL, but only the designated server can do that. From the chain alone you cannot tell what this material is.

roles.publisher: The account that ran publish — the wallet connected in the portal
roles.factory: Ocean's ERC721Factory. A shared contract already on Sepolia that mass-produces NFTs
roles.dataNft: The Data NFT created by this publish — the asset itself. Its DID is computed from this address
roles.datatoken: The access token created by this publish — a voucher representing the right to use the asset
roles.dispenser: The shared dispenser contract. It already existed; this publish only registered free distribution for this token
roles.nftTemplate: The NFT implementation template. The new NFT is a 45-byte stand-in that borrows this code
roles.erc20Template: The token implementation template, reused the same way
roles.feeToken: The reference token used for fee calculation
roles.marketFeeCollector: Where market fees would go. Set to zero here

actor.unknownEoa: An account with a key, not in this guide’s table
actor.unknownContract: A contract, not in this guide’s table

hint.from: Only accounts with a key can send transactions. Contracts cannot send on their own.
hint.to: What this transaction called. The first one calls the factory; the third calls the NFT itself — notice that the destination changes.
hint.block: The sequence number of the block this landed in. Sepolia advances one every ~12 seconds, and the number fixes the order.
hint.gas: Gas measures the work and storage; the price depends on how busy the network was.
hint.fee: Gas x price. Registering data alone reduces the publisher’s ETH.
hint.calldata: What the portal sent to the chain, including the encrypted DDO.
hint.logs: A single transaction can emit any number of records, because contracts call other contracts inside it.

calldata.title: Inside the calldata
calldata.lead: The arguments the portal sent to the chain. Anyone can read the bytes, but if they were encrypted before sending, the contents stay closed. Transaction 1 is entirely plain; transaction 3 is mostly an encrypted DDO.
calldata.plain: Everything sent in this transaction is plain text.
calldata.mixed: This transaction carries an encrypted blob in its calldata.

ddo.title: View the DDO (the document describing the asset)
ddo.lead: The chain holds only an encrypted blob. To see inside, you must ask the decryptor node recorded on chain. This card shows that dependency directly.
ddo.didNote: Derived mechanically from the NFT address and chain ID. Nobody assigns it.
ddo.ok: The node returned the DDO. This is the node’s decryption of it — not something read from the chain.
ddo.unreachable: The recorded decryptor cannot be reached. Either the server is down or it does not accept the connection. In this state nobody can tell the asset’s title or licence, even though the on-chain record is intact.
ddo.notIndexed: The node answered but has not indexed this asset yet. This is normal right after publishing.
ddo.noUrl: No decryptor is recorded in this transaction. It is recorded in the transaction that wrote the DDO.
ddo.blocked: The recorded URL points at a private network, so it is not requested (for safety).
ddo.files: Note: files (the data URLs) are encrypted a second time inside the DDO. Even the node’s decrypted DDO keeps them closed.
